Experiments in language evolution: inferences from closed- vs open-ended semantic space paradigms

Data modeling

analysis by Aleksandra Ćwiek

31 August, 2025

1 Introduction

Experiments in language evolution: inferences from closed- vs open-ended semantic space paradigms

Svetlana Kuleshova*1,2, Stefan Hartmann3, and Michael Pleyer1, Marta Sibierska1, Johan Blomberg4, Przemysław Żywiczyński1, Aleksandra Ćwiek5,1, Sławomir Wacewicz1

*Corresponding Author: 40010189@parisnanterre.fr

1Nicolaus Copernicus University in Toruń, Center for Language Evolution Studies, Fosa Staromiejska 3, 87-100 Toruń, Poland.

2ArScAn-Équipe AnTET (UMR 7041), CNRS, Université Paris Nanterre, 21 Allée de l’Université, 92000, Nanterre, France.

3Heinrich Heine University Düsseldorf, Faculty of Arts and Humanities, Universitätsstraße 1, 40225 Düsseldorf, Germany.

4Stockholm University, Department of Swedish and Multilingualism. Universitetsvägen 10, 106 91 Stockholm.

5Leibniz-Centre General Linguistics, Berlin, 10719, Germany

We challenge the validity of the multiple-choice paradigm used in many communication experiments. We replicated two experiments and replaced the original multiple-choice design with free-text answers. Our results indicate that participants performed worse compared to the original studies. The post hoc analysis showed that often relevant semantic domains were correctly identified, but full congruency with the target concepts was rare. We discuss how the results of each paradigm can be mapped onto a larger picture of language evolution.

What inferences about reality can we make from linguistic experiments? By definition, controlled experiments do not represent reality in all its complexity, and thus, it is important to be cautious when drawing conclusions. As one example, some recent experimental studies have made strong claims concluding that humans can understand improvised or interspecies forms of communication, specifically, novel non-linguistic vocalizations (Ćwiek et al., 2021) and gestures in non-human great apes (Graham and Hobaiter, 2023). Here, we follow up on these studies, altering one crucial aspect: Both original studies used a multiple-choice paradigm, whereby participants were constrained to choose one answer from a small set of alternatives; that is, for each gesture or vocalisation they were offered a set of potential interpretations and asked to guess the one best reflecting its intended meaning. We expected that replacing the closed-ended, multiple-choice paradigm with an open-ended, free-text paradigm would lead to different results and thus different conclusions about human capacities to ‘understand’ ape gestures or novel vocalizations.

To test our hypothesis, we replicated the studies by Ćwiek et al. and Graham & Hobaiter, but with the participants freely typing in their answer (i.e., their interpretation of the meaning of an ape gesture or novel vocalisation) rather than selecting it from a set of predefined choices. To assess the proximity of the participants’ answers with the target concepts, we used three complementary approaches: (i) binary assessment of correctness (yes/no), (ii) manual coding on a four-point scale, (iii) cosine similarity between the participants’ responses and the target concepts using ConceptNet. For (i) and (ii), participants’ answers were coded by two raters on a four-point Likert scale (transformed into a binary system for (i)), showing moderate-to-high inter-rater agreement. All mismatches between coders were discussed in the team and resolved. For (iii), the proximity between the words in the responses (heads of phrases in the case of multi-word answers) and the word denoting the target concept in ConceptNet (Speer et al. 2017) were assessed automatically. Across all approaches, our results show that participants performed qualitatively worse compared to the original studies, with a vast majority of responses showing no resemblance whatsoever to the target concept according to the manual coding procedure. In the ConceptNet analysis, the responses were found to be conceptually fairly close to the target concepts in many cases (e.g., the same semantic domain, as in ‘sleep’ vs ‘snore’), but hardly any response was fully congruent with the target concept.

Apart from revisiting the question to what extent participants “understand” novel vocalizations or ape gestures, our data give us the opportunity to evaluate different possibilities of interpreting participants’ free-text answers: manual coding with different levels of granularity on the one hand, and automatic similarity detection using NLP resources on the other. The three measures we used carve out different semantic landscapes, shaping how we perceive communicative transparency. A perfect-match approach treats meaning as a binary on/off switch, limiting “understanding” to exact hits while discarding near-misses as failures. The Likert-scale approach expands this space, recognizing perceived shades of similarity. The ConceptNet-based cosine similarity approach stretches the landscape even further, mapping words onto a gradient of conceptual distances, where even broad associations register as meaningful connections. Because these methods define similarity differently, they potentially reveal different facets of how novel signals convey meaning.

We thus conclude that different setups and analysis methods give us a nuanced perspective on the role of semantic space in semiotic experiments. These various paths to data collection and data treatment can inform a nuanced discussion of how experimental results can inform the evolution of today’s languages.

capTab <- function(x){
  if (outputFormat == 'html'){

  }

capFig <- function(x, show_R_version=FALSE, show_package_versions=NULL, is_map=FALSE){
  if (outputFormat == 'html'){
    assign(".last_fig_no", capFigNo, envir = .GlobalEnv) # remember current number
    x <- paste0("**Figure ", capFigNo, ".** ", x)
    capFigNo <<- capFigNo + 1L
  }
  x
}

# --- plot hook to auto-save ---
.default_plot_hook <- knitr::knit_hooks$get("plot")
.has_magick <- requireNamespace("magick", quietly = TRUE)

knitr::knit_hooks$set(plot = function(x, options){
  res <- if (is.function(.default_plot_hook)) .default_plot_hook(x, options) else NULL

  if (!is.null(options$fig.cap)) {
    fig_no <- get(".last_fig_no", envir = .GlobalEnv, inherits = FALSE)
    if (!is.na(fig_no)) {
      fig_no_str <- sprintf("%02d", fig_no)

      # subfolder = Rmd filename without extension
      rmd_name <- tools::file_path_sans_ext(basename(knitr::current_input()))
      target_dir <- file.path(plots, rmd_name)
      if (!dir.exists(target_dir)) dir.create(target_dir, recursive = TRUE)

      png_out <- file.path(target_dir, paste0("Figure_", fig_no_str, ".png"))
      tif_out <- file.path(target_dir, paste0("Figure_", fig_no_str, ".tif"))

      file.copy(x, png_out, overwrite = TRUE)

      if (.has_magick) {
        img <- magick::image_read(png_out)
        magick::image_write(img, path = tif_out, format = "tiff", compression = "lzw")
      } else {
        file.copy(png_out, tif_out, overwrite = TRUE)
      }
    }
  }

  res
})

Other helpers

bb_corr <- function(x, y, R = 4000, seed = 1708) {
  stopifnot(length(x) == length(y))
  set.seed(seed)
  n <- length(x)
  out <- numeric(R)
  for (r in seq_len(R)) {
    w <- rexp(n)          # Dirichlet via i.i.d. Exponential then normalize
    w <- w / sum(w)
    mx <- sum(w * x); my <- sum(w * y)
    sx <- sqrt(sum(w * (x - mx)^2))
    sy <- sqrt(sum(w * (y - my)^2))
    out[r] <- sum(w * (x - mx) * (y - my)) / (sx * sy)
  }
  out
}

summ_post <- function(draws, name){
  h <- hdi(draws, ci = 0.95)
  tibble(pair = name,
         mean = mean(draws),
         median = median(draws),
         hdi_low = h$CI_low,
         hdi_high = h$CI_high)
}

bf_bic <- function(y, x){
  fit1 <- lm(y ~ x)
  fit0 <- lm(y ~ 1)
  BIC0 <- BIC(fit0); BIC1 <- BIC(fit1)
  # BF10 ≈ exp((BIC0 - BIC1)/2)
  exp((BIC0 - BIC1)/2)
}

4 Modeling

4.1 Full (not implemented)

We first fit baseline models for each of the three measures, with only random intercepts for participant, native language, and stimulus. After baselines we’ll add cross-measure “coupling” models to test how measures relate (but aren’t identical), compare by LOO (and optionally Bayes factors via bridgesampling), and extract posteriors that demonstrate distinct yet overlapping semantic landscapes.

Full solution. (It will take days.)

{
  set.seed(1708)

  ## ---- ensure models dir exists (you already have `models` as an absolute path) ----
  if (!dir.exists(models)) dir.create(models, recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)

  ## ---- data prep (minimal; no z-scoring of cosine) ----
  if (!"ord_norm" %in% names(df)) df$ord_norm <- df$judged_similarity / 3
  df_brm <- df
  df_brm$participant      <- factor(df_brm$participant)
  df_brm$stimulus_concept <- factor(df_brm$stimulus_concept)
  df_brm$native_language  <- factor(df_brm$native_language) # decided to do without it because it was not variable and caused much longer computation times
  df_brm$judged_ord       <- factor(df_brm$judged_similarity, levels = 0:3, ordered = TRUE)
 # Replace values extremely close to 1 with exactly 1
  df_brm$cosine_rescaled <- ifelse(
    !is.na(df_brm$cosine_rescaled) & df_brm$cosine_rescaled > 1 & df_brm$cosine_rescaled <
      1.001,
    1,
    df_brm$cosine_rescaled
  )
  
  ## ---- very wide priors for baselines / couplings (not for ZOIB components) ----
  .pri_bin <- c(
    set_prior("normal(0, 5)", class = "Intercept"),
    #set_prior("normal(0, 2)", class = "b"),
    set_prior("student_t(3, 0, 5)", class = "sd")
  )
  .pri_ord <- c(
    set_prior("normal(0, 5)", class = "Intercept"),  # thresholds
    #set_prior("normal(0, 2)", class = "b"),
    set_prior("student_t(3, 0, 5)", class = "sd")
  )
  .pri_wide <- c(
    set_prior("normal(0, 5)", class = "Intercept"),
    #set_prior("normal(0, 2)", class = "b"),
    set_prior("student_t(3, 0, 5)", class = "sd")
  )

  ## ========================= BASELINES =========================
  .bin_rds <- file.path(models, "fit_bin.rds")
  if (file.exists(.bin_rds)) {
    fit_bin <- readRDS(.bin_rds)
  } else {
    fit_bin <- brm(
      binary_guess ~ 1 + (1|p|participant) + (1|s|stimulus_concept),
      data    = df_brm,
      family  = bernoulli(),
      prior   = .pri_bin,
      chains  = 4, iter = 8000, warmup = 4000,
      control = list(adapt_delta = 0.97, max_treedepth = 12),
      seed    = 1708, refresh = 100,
      save_pars = save_pars(all = TRUE)
    )
    saveRDS(fit_bin, .bin_rds)
  }

  .ord_rds <- file.path(models, "fit_ord.rds")
  if (file.exists(.ord_rds)) {
    fit_ord <- readRDS(.ord_rds)
  } else {
    fit_ord <- brm(
      judged_ord ~ 1 + (1|p|participant) + (1|s|stimulus_concept),
      data    = df_brm,
      family  = cumulative(link = "logit"),
      prior   = .pri_ord,
      chains  = 4, iter = 8000, warmup = 4000,
      control = list(adapt_delta = 0.97, max_treedepth = 12),
      seed    = 1708, refresh = 100,
      save_pars = save_pars(all = TRUE)
    )
    saveRDS(fit_ord, .ord_rds)
  }

  .cos_rds <- file.path(models, "fit_cos.rds")
  if (file.exists(.cos_rds)) {
    fit_cos <- readRDS(.cos_rds)
  } else {
    fit_cos <- brm(
      cosine_rescaled ~ 1 + (1|p|participant) + (1|s|stimulus_concept),
      data    = df_brm,
      family  = zero_one_inflated_beta(),  # includes exact 0s and 1s
      # per your rule: no explicit priors for ZOIB subcomponents
      chains  = 4, iter = 8000, warmup = 4000,
      control = list(adapt_delta = 0.97, max_treedepth = 12),
      seed    = 1708, refresh = 100,
      save_pars = save_pars(all = TRUE)
    )
    saveRDS(fit_cos, .cos_rds)
  }

  ## ---- compact Bayes R^2 (kept as r2_table) ----
  .r2 <- function(fit) { r <- bayes_R2(fit); c(Estimate = mean(r), Q2.5 = quantile(r,.025), Q97.5 = quantile(r,.975)) }
  r2_table <- data.frame(
    model = c("Binary (Bernoulli)", "Judged (Ordinal)", "Cosine (ZOIB)"),
    rbind(.r2(fit_bin), .r2(fit_ord), .r2(fit_cos))
  )
  rownames(r2_table) <- NULL
  r2_table$Estimate <- round(r2_table$Estimate, 3)
  r2_table$Q2.5     <- round(r2_table$Q2.5, 3)
  r2_table$Q97.5    <- round(r2_table$Q97.5, 3)
  print(r2_table)

  ## ========================= COUPLING MODELS =========================
  ## Judged <- Cosine (no z-scoring; cosine_rescaled is 0–1 and interpretable)
  .m_ord_cos_rds <- file.path(models, "m_ord_cos.rds")
  if (file.exists(.m_ord_cos_rds)) {
    m_ord_cos <- readRDS(.m_ord_cos_rds)
  } else {
    m_ord_cos <- brm(
      judged_ord ~ 1 + cosine_rescaled +
        (1 + cosine_rescaled | s | stimulus_concept) +
        (1 | p | participant) + (1 | l | native_language),
      data    = df_brm, family = cumulative("logit"),
      prior   = .pri_wide,
      chains  = 4, iter = 8000, warmup = 4000,
      control = list(adapt_delta = 0.98, max_treedepth = 13),
      seed    = 1708, refresh = 50,
      save_pars = save_pars(all = TRUE)
    )
    saveRDS(m_ord_cos, .m_ord_cos_rds)
  }

  ## Binary <- Cosine
  .m_bin_cos_rds <- file.path(models, "m_bin_cos.rds")
  if (file.exists(.m_bin_cos_rds)) {
    m_bin_cos <- readRDS(.m_bin_cos_rds)
  } else {
    m_bin_cos <- brm(
      binary_guess ~ 1 + cosine_rescaled +
        (1 + cosine_rescaled | s | stimulus_concept) +
        (1 | p | participant) + (1 | l | native_language),
      data    = df_brm, family = bernoulli(),
      prior   = .pri_wide,
      chains  = 4, iter = 8000, warmup = 4000,
      control = list(adapt_delta = 0.98, max_treedepth = 13),
      seed    = 1708, refresh = 50,
      save_pars = save_pars(all = TRUE)
    )
    saveRDS(m_bin_cos, .m_bin_cos_rds)
  }

  ## Binary <- Judged (uses your 0–1 'ord_norm')
  .m_bin_jud_rds <- file.path(models, "m_bin_jud.rds")
  if (file.exists(.m_bin_jud_rds)) {
    m_bin_jud <- readRDS(.m_bin_jud_rds)
  } else {
    m_bin_jud <- brm(
      binary_guess ~ 1 + ord_norm +
        (1 + ord_norm | s | stimulus_concept) +
        (1 | p | participant) + (1 | l | native_language),
      data    = df_brm, family = bernoulli(),
      prior   = .pri_wide,
      chains  = 4, iter = 8000, warmup = 4000,
      control = list(adapt_delta = 0.98, max_treedepth = 13),
      seed    = 1708, refresh = 50,
      save_pars = save_pars(all = TRUE)
    )
    saveRDS(m_bin_jud, .m_bin_jud_rds)
  }

  ## Cosine (ZOIB, μ) <- Judged (keep zoi/oi intercept-only)
  .m_cos_jud_rds <- file.path(models, "m_cos_jud.rds")
  if (file.exists(.m_cos_jud_rds)) {
    m_cos_jud <- readRDS(.m_cos_jud_rds)
  } else {
    m_cos_jud <- brm(
      cosine_rescaled ~ 1 + ord_norm +
        (1 + ord_norm | s | stimulus_concept) +
        (1 | p | participant) + (1 | l | native_language),
      data    = df_brm, family = zero_one_inflated_beta(),
      # no explicit priors for ZOIB components per your instruction
      chains  = 4, iter = 8000, warmup = 4000,
      control = list(adapt_delta = 0.98, max_treedepth = 13),
      seed    = 1708, refresh = 50,
      save_pars = save_pars(all = TRUE)
    )
    saveRDS(m_cos_jud, .m_cos_jud_rds)
  }

  ## ---- LOO comparisons (vs respective baselines) ----
  cat("\n# LOO: Binary baseline vs Binary <- Cosine\n")
  print(loo_compare(loo(fit_bin), loo(m_bin_cos)))
  cat("\n# LOO: Binary baseline vs Binary <- Judged\n")
  print(loo_compare(loo(fit_bin), loo(m_bin_jud)))
  cat("\n# LOO: Ordinal baseline vs Judged <- Cosine\n")
  print(loo_compare(loo(fit_ord), loo(m_ord_cos)))
  cat("\n# LOO: Cosine baseline vs Cosine <- Judged (ZOIB)\n")
  print(loo_compare(loo(fit_cos), loo(m_cos_jud)))

  ## ---- cleanup helpers (keep only model objects + r2_table + path vars) ----
  rm(list = c(".pri_bin",".pri_ord",".pri_wide",
              ".bin_rds",".ord_rds",".cos_rds",
              ".m_ord_cos_rds",".m_bin_cos_rds",".m_bin_jud_rds",".m_cos_jud_rds"))
}

4.2 Compromise

Compromise to meet computational time.

-     We keep the 1’s from cosine similarity conceptually (they’re just ε below 1 for Beta math), preserving order and near-perfect matches. Also rescaling to true 0-1 range (not positively skewed with much higher mean due to the nature of cosine similarity scale).

-     All three outcomes are on comparable 0–1 scales (binary 0/1, judged 0–1, cosine ε-open (0,1)), so the per-stimulus posterior means can be min–max rescaled to overlay the three “landscapes” directly (same axis).
  
-     Fast & robust: Bernoulli + Gaussian + Beta are far lighter than cumulative + ZOIB at N=27k, but they still answer the main question: the measures are related but not identical, visible in the differing shapes/ranks of stim_landscapes_scaled.
{
  set.seed(1708)

  ## ---------- ensure models dir exists ----------
  if (!dir.exists(models)) dir.create(models, recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)

  ## ---------- COMPLETE-CASE DATA (based on cosine) ----------
  # Rationale: use the same rows for all three outcomes to enable direct comparability
  df_cc <- subset(df, !is.na(cosine_rescaled))
  if (!"ord_norm" %in% names(df_cc)) df_cc$ord_norm <- df_cc$judged_similarity / 3

  df_cc$participant      <- factor(df_cc$participant)
  df_cc$stimulus_concept <- factor(df_cc$stimulus_concept)

  ## Keep exact-1 spike info for reporting (from original column but CC rows)
  ones_table_stim <- aggregate(I(df_cc$cosine_rescaled == 1) ~ stimulus_concept, data = df_cc, FUN = mean)
  names(ones_table_stim) <- c("stimulus_concept", "one_rate")

  ## ---------- Cosine transform: epsilon-open + unit-stretch ----------
  eps  <- 1e-10
  tiny <- 1e-12
  x    <- df_cc$cosine_rescaled
  x_open <- pmin(pmax(x - eps, tiny), 1 - tiny)
  xmin <- min(x_open, na.rm = TRUE); xmax <- max(x_open, na.rm = TRUE); span <- xmax - xmin
  if (!is.finite(span) || span <= 0) stop("Cosine span after opening is zero; cannot scale.")
  df_cc$cosine_unit_open <- pmin(pmax((x_open - xmin) / span, tiny), 1 - tiny)

  ## ---------- very wide priors (intercept + RE sd only) ----------
  .pri_intercepts_only <- c(
    set_prior("normal(0, 5)", class = "Intercept"),
    set_prior("student_t(3, 0, 5)", class = "sd")
  )

  ## =================================================================
  ##                           BASELINES (fast, CC)
  ## =================================================================
  ctrl_strict <- list(adapt_delta = 0.99, max_treedepth = 13)

  ## 1) Binary (Bernoulli) on df_cc
  .bin_cc_rds <- file.path(models, "fit_bin_cc.rds")
  if (file.exists(.bin_cc_rds)) {
    fit_bin_cc <- readRDS(.bin_cc_rds)
  } else {
    fit_bin_cc <- brm(
      binary_guess ~ 1 + (1|p|participant) + (1|s|stimulus_concept),
      data    = df_cc,
      family  = bernoulli(),
      prior   = .pri_intercepts_only,
      chains  = 4, iter = 8000, warmup = 4000,
      control = ctrl_strict,
      seed    = 1708, refresh = 100,
      save_pars = save_pars(all = TRUE)
    )
    saveRDS(fit_bin_cc, .bin_cc_rds)
  }

  ## 2) Judged (Gaussian 0–1) on df_cc
  .ord_cc_rds <- file.path(models, "fit_ord_gauss_cc.rds")
  if (file.exists(.ord_cc_rds)) {
    fit_ord_gauss_cc <- readRDS(.ord_cc_rds)
  } else {
    fit_ord_gauss_cc <- brm(
      ord_norm ~ 1 + (1|p|participant) + (1|s|stimulus_concept),
      data    = df_cc,
      family  = gaussian(),
      prior   = .pri_intercepts_only,
      chains  = 4, iter = 8000, warmup = 4000,
      control = ctrl_strict,
      seed    = 1708, refresh = 100,
      save_pars = save_pars(all = TRUE)
    )
    saveRDS(fit_ord_gauss_cc, .ord_cc_rds)
  }

  ## 3) Cosine (Beta on unit-stretched) on df_cc
  .cos_cc_rds <- file.path(models, "fit_cos_beta_unit_cc.rds")
  if (file.exists(.cos_cc_rds)) {
    fit_cos_beta_cc <- readRDS(.cos_cc_rds)
  } else {
    fit_cos_beta_cc <- brm(
      cosine_unit_open ~ 1 + (1|p|participant) + (1|s|stimulus_concept),
      data    = df_cc,
      family  = Beta(),
      prior   = .pri_intercepts_only,
      chains  = 4, iter = 8000, warmup = 4000,
      control = ctrl_strict,
      seed    = 1708, refresh = 100,
      save_pars = save_pars(all = TRUE)
    )
    saveRDS(fit_cos_beta_cc, .cos_cc_rds)
  }

  ## ================== ROBUST R² (cache to RDS) ==================
  .recalc_r2 <- FALSE  # set TRUE to force recomputation

  .r2_tbl_rds <- file.path(models, "r2_table_cc.rds")
  .r2_bin_rds <- file.path(models, "r2_draws_bin_cc.rds")
  .r2_ord_rds <- file.path(models, "r2_draws_ord_cc.rds")
  .r2_cos_rds <- file.path(models, "r2_draws_cos_cc.rds")

  if (!.recalc_r2 &&
      file.exists(.r2_tbl_rds) &&
      file.exists(.r2_bin_rds) &&
      file.exists(.r2_ord_rds) &&
      file.exists(.r2_cos_rds)) {

    r2_bin <- readRDS(.r2_bin_rds)
    r2_ord <- readRDS(.r2_ord_rds)
    r2_cos <- readRDS(.r2_cos_rds)
    r2_table_cc <- readRDS(.r2_tbl_rds)

  } else {

    r2_bin <- bayes_R2(fit_bin_cc)       # numeric vector of draws
    r2_ord <- bayes_R2(fit_ord_gauss_cc)
    r2_cos <- bayes_R2(fit_cos_beta_cc)

    saveRDS(r2_bin, .r2_bin_rds)
    saveRDS(r2_ord, .r2_ord_rds)
    saveRDS(r2_cos, .r2_cos_rds)

    .summ <- function(x) c(Estimate = mean(x),
                           `Q2.5`   = as.numeric(quantile(x, .025)),
                           `Q97.5`  = as.numeric(quantile(x, .975)))
    r2_table_cc <- rbind(.summ(r2_bin), .summ(r2_ord), .summ(r2_cos))
    r2_table_cc <- as.data.frame(r2_table_cc)
    r2_table_cc <- tibble::rownames_to_column(r2_table_cc, "Model")
    r2_table_cc <- dplyr::mutate(r2_table_cc, dplyr::across(where(is.numeric), ~round(.x, 3)))
    r2_table_cc$Model <- c("Binary (Bernoulli, CC)",
                           "Judged (Gaussian 0–1, CC)",
                           "Cosine (Beta, unit-stretched, CC)")

    saveRDS(r2_table_cc, .r2_tbl_rds)
  }

  print(r2_table_cc)

  ## ================== PER-STIMULUS POSTERIOR MEANS (CC) ==================
  stim_levels_cc <- levels(df_cc$stimulus_concept)
  new_stim_cc <- data.frame(stimulus_concept = stim_levels_cc)

  # Binary: marginal over participant; keep only stimulus RE
  bin_pred <- as.data.frame(
    fitted(fit_bin_cc, newdata = new_stim_cc, re_formula = ~(1|s|stimulus_concept), summary = TRUE)
  )
  bin_stim <- data.frame(stimulus_concept = stim_levels_cc, bin_mean = bin_pred$Estimate)

  # Judged (Gaussian)
  ord_pred <- as.data.frame(
    fitted(fit_ord_gauss_cc, newdata = new_stim_cc, re_formula = ~(1|s|stimulus_concept), summary = TRUE)
  )
  ord_stim <- data.frame(stimulus_concept = stim_levels_cc, ord_mean = ord_pred$Estimate)

  # Cosine (Beta)
  cos_pred <- as.data.frame(
    fitted(fit_cos_beta_cc, newdata = new_stim_cc, re_formula = ~(1|s|stimulus_concept), summary = TRUE)
  )
  cos_stim <- data.frame(stimulus_concept = stim_levels_cc, cos_mean = cos_pred$Estimate)

  # Merge + add spike info (computed on CC rows)
  suppressWarnings({
    stim_landscapes_cc <- dplyr::left_join(bin_stim, ord_stim, by = "stimulus_concept") |>
      dplyr::left_join(cos_stim, by = "stimulus_concept") |>
      dplyr::left_join(ones_table_stim, by = "stimulus_concept")
  })

  # Min–max rescale summaries (for plotting; does not affect models)
  mm <- function(v) (v - min(v, na.rm = TRUE)) / (max(v, na.rm = TRUE) - min(v, na.rm = TRUE))
  stim_landscapes_cc_scaled <- transform(
    stim_landscapes_cc,
    bin_mm = mm(bin_mean),
    ord_mm = mm(ord_mean),
    cos_mm = mm(cos_mean)
  )

  ## ---------- keep useful objects ----------
  assign("df_cc", df_cc, inherits = FALSE)
  assign("fit_bin_cc", fit_bin_cc, inherits = FALSE)
  assign("fit_ord_gauss_cc", fit_ord_gauss_cc, inherits = FALSE)
  assign("fit_cos_beta_cc", fit_cos_beta_cc, inherits = FALSE)
  assign("r2_table_cc", r2_table_cc, inherits = FALSE)
  assign("r2_draws_cc", list(Binary = r2_bin, Judged = r2_ord, Cosine = r2_cos), inherits = FALSE)
  assign("stim_landscapes_cc", stim_landscapes_cc, inherits = FALSE)
  assign("stim_landscapes_cc_scaled", stim_landscapes_cc_scaled, inherits = FALSE)

  ## ---------- cleanup helpers ----------
  rm(.pri_intercepts_only, .bin_cc_rds, .ord_cc_rds, .cos_cc_rds,
     .r2_tbl_rds, .r2_bin_rds, .r2_ord_rds, .r2_cos_rds,
     .r2_summ, stim_levels_cc, new_stim_cc, bin_pred, ord_pred, cos_pred, mm,
     ones_table_stim, eps, tiny, x, x_open, xmin, xmax, span, ctrl_strict)
}

4.2.1 Extract results

Bayesian R² for each fitted model using bayes_R2(). This is a quick, comparable goodness-of-fit summary.

r2_table_cc

Posterior predictive checks for all three models, shown side-by-side for quick visual comparison. If patchwork is available we combine them horizontally; otherwise they will print one after another. No captions, so nothing gets copied out by your hook.

suppressWarnings(has_patchwork <- requireNamespace("patchwork", quietly = TRUE))

p_bin  <- pp_check(fit_bin_cc,       ndraws = 200) + ggtitle("Binary (Bernoulli)")
p_gaus <- pp_check(fit_ord_gauss_cc, ndraws = 200) + ggtitle("Judged (Gaussian 0–1)")
p_beta <- pp_check(fit_cos_beta_cc,  ndraws = 200) + ggtitle("Cosine (Beta)")

if (has_patchwork) {
  patchwork::wrap_plots(p_bin, p_gaus, p_beta, ncol = 3)
} else {
  print(p_bin); print(p_gaus); print(p_beta)
}

4.3 Posteriors visualized

# Descriptive posterior summaries for intercepts (μ) + pairwise probabilities

# --- Helper: posterior draws of μ on outcome scale (drop all REs)
.post_mu_draws <- function(fit, label, ref_row = 1) {
  mu <- fitted(fit, newdata = df_cc[ref_row, , drop = TRUE],
               re_formula = NA, summary = FALSE)
  tibble(model = label, mu = as.numeric(mu))
}

# --- Get/assemble draws (ordered Binary -> Judged -> Cosine)
mu_draws <- bind_rows(
  .post_mu_draws(fit_bin_cc,       "Binary guess"),
  .post_mu_draws(fit_ord_gauss_cc, "Judged similarity"),
  .post_mu_draws(fit_cos_beta_cc,  "Cosine similarity")
) %>%
  mutate(model = factor(model,
                        levels = c("Binary guess", "Judged similarity", "Cosine similarity")))

# --- Summary table for manuscript (median, mean, 95% CrI)
mu_summary <- mu_draws %>%
  group_by(model) %>%
  summarise(
    mean   = mean(mu),
    median = median(mu),
    `Q2.5` = quantile(mu, .025),
    `Q97.5`= quantile(mu, .975),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

# Optional: friendly formatting for tiny numbers
fmt_num <- function(x) {
  out <- ifelse(x < 0.001, formatC(x, format = "e", digits = 2),
                ifelse(x < 0.01,  formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 3),
                                 formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 3)))
  as.character(out)
}

mu_summary_print <- mu_summary %>%
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), fmt_num)) %>%
  rename(`Model` = model,
         `Mean μ` = mean, `Median μ` = median,
         `2.5%` = `Q2.5`, `97.5%` = `Q97.5`)

cat("\nIntercept (population mean μ on outcome scale) — posterior summaries:\n")
## 
## Intercept (population mean μ on outcome scale) — posterior summaries:
knitr::kable(mu_summary_print, align = "lcccc")
Model Mean μ Median μ 2.5% 97.5%
Binary guess 0.001 8.41e-04 1.67e-04 0.003
Judged similarity 0.074 0.074 0.015 0.134
Cosine similarity 0.362 0.361 0.292 0.436 
# --- Pairwise comparisons: P(mu_A > mu_B) & posterior for differences
# We pair draws by random sampling to a common length for each comparison.
set.seed(1708)

get_draws_for <- function(lbl) filter(mu_draws, model == lbl) %>% pull(mu)

d_bin  <- get_draws_for("Binary guess")
d_judg <- get_draws_for("Judged similarity")
d_cos  <- get_draws_for("Cosine similarity")

pair_prob <- function(x, y, n = 10000L) {
  n <- min(length(x), length(y), n)
  ix <- sample(seq_along(x), n, replace = length(x) < n)
  iy <- sample(seq_along(y), n, replace = length(y) < n)
  dx <- y[iy] - x[ix]               # positive => y > x
  tibble(
    n = n,
    diff_median = median(dx),
    diff_q2.5   = quantile(dx, .025),
    diff_q97.5  = quantile(dx, .975),
    P_y_gt_x    = mean(dx > 0)
  )
}

cmp_list <- list(
  `Judged − Binary` = pair_prob(d_bin, d_judg),
  `Cosine − Binary` = pair_prob(d_bin, d_cos),
  `Cosine − Judged` = pair_prob(d_judg, d_cos)
)

pairwise_summary <- bind_rows(cmp_list, .id = "Comparison")

pairwise_print <- pairwise_summary %>%
  mutate(
    across(c(diff_median, diff_q2.5, diff_q97.5), fmt_num),
    `P(Second > First)` = formatC(P_y_gt_x, format = "f", digits = 3)
  ) %>%
  select(Comparison,
         `P(Second > First)`,
         `Diff median` = diff_median,
         `Diff 2.5%`   = diff_q2.5,
         `Diff 97.5%`  = diff_q97.5,
         n)

cat("\nPairwise comparisons of intercepts μ (posterior on differences and probabilities):\n")
## 
## Pairwise comparisons of intercepts μ (posterior on differences and probabilities):
knitr::kable(pairwise_print, align = "lccccr")
Comparison P(Second > First) Diff median Diff 2.5% Diff 97.5% n
Judged − Binary 0.991 0.072 0.015 0.132 10000
Cosine − Binary 1.000 0.360 0.290 0.437 10000
Cosine − Judged 1.000 0.287 0.197 0.382 10000 
# --- Keep tidy objects for later use/exports
assign("mu_draws",    mu_draws,    inherits = FALSE)
assign("mu_summary",  mu_summary,  inherits = FALSE)
assign("pairwise_summary", pairwise_summary, inherits = FALSE)

4.4 Semantic landscape!

stopifnot(exists("cats"), exists("df_cc"),
          exists("fit_bin_cc"), exists("fit_ord_gauss_cc"), exists("fit_cos_beta_cc"))

# helper: per-stimulus posterior mean on OUTCOME scale, stimulus RE only
.get_stim <- function(fit, label) {
  nd <- data.frame(stimulus_concept = levels(df_cc$stimulus_concept))
  f  <- fitted(fit, newdata = nd, re_formula = ~(1|s|stimulus_concept), summary = TRUE)
  tibble(
    meaning = nd$stimulus_concept,
    mean    = f[, "Estimate"],
    lo      = f[, "Q2.5"],
    hi      = f[, "Q97.5"],
    measure = label
  )
}

# long → wide with subcategory
stim_means_long <- bind_rows(
  .get_stim(fit_bin_cc,       "Binary guess"),
  .get_stim(fit_ord_gauss_cc, "Judged similarity"),
  .get_stim(fit_cos_beta_cc,  "Cosine similarity")
) %>%
  left_join(cats, by = "meaning")

stim_means_wide <- stim_means_long %>%
  select(meaning, subcategory, measure, mean) %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = measure, values_from = mean) %>%
  rename(binary = `Binary guess`,
         judged = `Judged similarity`,
         cosine = `Cosine similarity`)

# subcategory centroids (means across stimuli in each subcategory)
subcat_wide <- stim_means_wide %>%
  group_by(subcategory) %>%
  summarise(
    n_stim = dplyr::n(),
    binary = mean(binary, na.rm = TRUE),
    judged = mean(judged, na.rm = TRUE),
    cosine = mean(cosine, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    # contrasts (heights) that capture the "gaps" between lenses
    cos_minus_jud = cosine - judged,   # distributional advantage over human-graded
    jud_minus_bin = judged - binary,   # graded advantage over strict hits
    dom = c("Binary","Judged","Cosine")[max.col(cbind(binary, judged, cosine), ties.method = "first")],
    dom = factor(dom, levels = c("Binary","Judged","Cosine"))
  )

assign("stim_means_wide", stim_means_wide, inherits = FALSE)
assign("subcat_wide", subcat_wide, inherits = FALSE)

For each subcategory, show two horizontal contrasts on a common zero line: Judged − Binary (how much graded ratings exceed strict hits) and Cosine − Judged (how much distributional proximity exceeds human ratings). This makes the “landscape differences” explicit and comparable. Subcategories are sorted by Cosine − Judged so the eye immediately catches where distributional semantics adds the most.

Judged − Binary > 0 → allowing graded human judgments uncovers structure ignored by exact hits.

Cosine − Judged > 0 → distributional proximity recognises neighborhood-level meaning beyond human “similarity” ratings.

Both > 0 → a clear gradient: Binary < Judged < Cosine for that subcategory.

Negative values (no such cases) → the earlier lens explains more than the later one.

Figure 8. Subcategory Advantage Grid. For each subcategory, the right-facing bar shows Cosine − Judged (distributional advantage) and the left/right bar shows Judged − Binary (graded advantage over exact hits). Bars to the right of zero indicate the second measure exceeds the first. Point size encodes the number of stimuli in the subcategory. Interpretation: where both bars are large and positive, free-text responses are captured poorly by binary hits but progressively better by human grading and best by distributional proximity.

Figure 9. Semantic topography of similarity measures. The plot renders the difference between distributional (cosine) and human-judged similarity as a topographic surface in Judged (x) × Cosine (y) space. Blue “elevations” indicate regions where cosine similarity assigns higher values than human ratings, while red “depressions” show the reverse. The dashed line marks equality (Cos = Jud). Black-rimmed points are subcategory centroids, scaled by their Binary μ (proportion of exact matches). This visualization highlights how different measures carve out distinct semantic landscapes: binary exact hits are rare (small capitals), judged similarity introduces a gradient, and cosine expands the landscape further by capturing semantic neighborhoods beyond human ratings.

Figure 10. Each subcategory’s centroid in Judged (x) × Cosine (y) becomes a “capital.” We tessellate the plane into Voronoi regions, coloring each “country” by Cosine − Judged (blue = distributional advantage; red = judged advantage). Point size shows Binary μ (strict hits), and labels name the subcategories. The dashed 45° line marks equality. This gives a true map where borders reflect which centroid is closest; visually, you get semantic “territories” defined by graded measures, with color/topography conveying which lens is more permissive.
